summary: Which qualities drive the design, and which words in a kata point to each one.

items.when: "Must continue to work when…", or money lost each minute down
Large or growing user numbers, plans to expand
Load that jumps: a sale opens, a storm, the lunch hour
"Real time", "immediately", users who wait on a screen
Weak networks, external systems that go offline
A small team, a small budget, a short deadline

blocks.title: Signals of data, rules, and change

items.when: "Must never sell one seat twice", money, stock, legal records
Payments, health data, personal data, bots
Frequent changes, many teams, staged rollouts
"Next year we want to add…", new countries, new partners
Existing systems, partners, several external parties

blocks.title: Characteristics that are easy to mix up
rows: Is up when users need it
Continues, possibly with fewer functions, when one part fails
Handles more users or data as the business grows
Handles sudden peaks, then releases the capacity

items.text: A characteristic is a quality of the system, not a feature.
"Customers pay online" is a feature. "Payment works during the lunch peak" is elasticity.
The characteristics you select decide the style.
Other names for characteristics: non-functional requirements and quality attributes.
Select the few that drive the design, and tie each one to a sentence in the kata.
Three is the usual number. The app lets you select up to five.
A design that tries to be good at everything is good at nothing.
Compare options against the three driving characteristics, plus cost and team skills.

items.when: Modules must change and deploy alone
items.use: A cycle check, for example ArchUnit

items.when: Domain code must not import web code
items.use: A layer rule, for example dependency-cruiser

items.when: A latency target must hold before each release
items.use: A p99 threshold in a pipeline load test

items.when: Latency must hold under real traffic
items.use: An SLO with an error budget alert
A dependency scan on each build

items.when: No service must read the tables of another service
items.use: A check of database users against tables

items.when: Requests must succeed when one copy stops
items.use: A scheduled test that stops one copy

items.text: Turn each important characteristic into a number. Then put an automatic check on the number.
Write down implicit characteristics, such as security, when the system needs more than the normal level.
Use percentiles, not averages. An average hides the slow requests.
State the load with each target. "p99 below 300 ms" means nothing without it.
Break a composite, such as agility, into parts that you can measure. Give each part a target.
Agree on each definition with the team and the business. Record it in an ADR.
A build test is atomic, triggered, and static. A p99 alert in production is continual and dynamic.
Run the checks in the same build as the tests. Make each failure explain the rule and the reason.
Write the characteristics for each quantum. Only the parts that need a strict target pay for it.
A rule only in a document breaks in months. A measure that becomes a target stops being useful.

blocks.title: Three kinds of measure
rows: Cyclomatic complexity, cycles between modules, coupling
Deploy frequency, time to deploy, failed deploys, test coverage

items.label: Cyclomatic complexity of a function
items.note: Each if, loop, case, &&, or || is a decision.

items.label: Complexity limit for each function
items.note: McCabe's rule of thumb. Teams often set a lower limit.
